t: A nomadic confederation joined herding tribes under one ruling clan and khan, and organised the whole people as an army in units of ten, a hundred, a thousand and ten thousand.
Steppe rulers lived largely on what they drew from settled empires by raids, tribute treaties and trade, as the Xiongnu did from Han China and Attila’s Huns from Constantinople.
Disputed successions repeatedly split these empires, and by 1757 the guns, forts and frontier treaties of Qing China and Russia had left the steppe no room for another.
dyk: According to the Book of Han, Han envoys could enter the Xiongnu ruler’s tents only after setting aside their tallies of office and having their faces tattooed; the envoy Wang Wu agreed and was received with honour.
ev: Modu Chanyu takes power and unites the Xiongnu, founding the first great empire of the eastern steppe
After Emperor Gaozu’s defeat at Baideng, the Han buy peace with a princess and regular gifts of silk and grain
Amid a Xiongnu civil war, Huhanye pays homage in person at Chang’an and accepts Han overlordship
Bumin Qaghan overthrows the Rouran and founds the First Turkic Khaganate
A kurultai at the source of the Onon river proclaims Temüjin Genghis Khan of the Mongols
Rival kurultais elect Kublai Khan and Ariq Böke as Great Khan, and the Mongol Empire begins to break apart
Qing armies crush the last Dzungar resistance, ending the last great nomadic empire of the steppe

f.power: A supreme ruler from one ruling clan (the Xiongnu chanyu, a khagan or khan), with princes, tribal chiefs and appointed commanders governing the wings and units of the army
f.legitimacy: A mandate from Heaven (Tengri) granted to the ruling clan, proved by victory and by the plunder, tribute and trade the ruler shared with his followers
f.chosen: Raised by an assembly of the ruling family and chiefs, the Mongol kurultai, from among the founder’s descendants, often after a contest among kinsmen decided by war
f.examples: the Xiongnu Empire (209 BCE–48 CE), the Hunnic Empire under Attila, the First Turkic Khaganate (552–603), the Uyghur Khaganate (744–840), the Mongol Empire (1206–1368), the Dzungar Khanate (1634–1757)
